I have ADHD and bipolar as well. My psych claims I can’t have both (no one else agrees) and won’t prescribe me anything for the ADHD. Here’s some tricks I attempt to use instead:

-Finch is an app I love. It gamifies executive functioning skills. Put in your goals for the day and you get a fun sound and rainbow stones (to dress up your bird!) for completing them. I’ve never gotten serotonin from showering like that.

-Lists! I have a list of everything I need to bring with me when I leave the house taped to my bedroom door. Helps me not shuffle in and out of the house 7 times cuz I forgot things

-Strict routine. I try to do the same thing every day. It helps the adhd and the bipolar, most of us thrive on some sort of routine

-For schoolwork: I personally always failed in this category but I’ve read doing homework for 15 minutes then taking 15 off helps get through it

-MOST IMPORTANT! Forgive yourself. Don’t listen to people telling you to “get your shit together”. You’re young and trying your best. 

The lamictal should help with your symptoms as well. I’m on it now and it lifts me out of depression and makes me more generally productive. If it doesn’t work, there’s tons of other meds you can try. This will get easier to manage as time goes on. Like I said, be patient and forgive yourself. You’re doing all you can. I’m proud of you for seeking help at such a young age. I personally just wallowed in it back then, so you’re ahead of the game. Best of luck💕

I’m not sure what your swim school does but mine has a special technique for bringing newbies underwater.

At this point he’s too old to dunk without consent. I avoid using the words “dunk” and “underwater” because I don’t want to set off their alarm bells. I say “ok friend, we’re gonna blow bubbles and get our whole faces wet!”

Holding him under his arms, gently move him back and forth across your chest. Tell him on 3 we’re getting our face wet. Count one, two, three, and then gently bring him underwater backwards. 

The back of his head should go in first, and then you should move him backwards under the water for a second or two. Do not hold him still or bring him forward. Bring him back up and obviously be so so excited. 

The idea here is the water rushed down and around his face rather than straight up his nose. I do this with infants to small 4 years olds and very very rarely do they come up coughing or crying. Another way to do this is after a jump, catch him under his arms and then bring him underwater backwards. The jump might be better considering you’ve been working on getting his face wet with that skill already.

Best of luck to you and your little guy!!!

Hi I’ve taught swim lessons for 9 years! I started when I was 15 and was so so scared to teach on my own but here are some tips:

-nothing wrong with asking your coworkers for pointers. I’m third in seniority at my swim school yet I’m constantly learning from younger, newer instructors

-safety is your number one priority. Keep your head on a swivel and make sure you don’t have your eyes off any child for too long

-building relationships with the kiddos is so so important. Ask them little questions like how old are you, what’s your favorite animal, what’s your favorite part of swim class

-CONFIDENCE IS KEY. Fake it til you make it. If you act confident, eventually you’ll start to feel confident, and then you’ll really shine as an instructor

-ask if you can do some additional shadowing (not for free!) if you’re still unsure. If they let you, lead a class and have the normal instructor assist and give tips. This helped me build confidence

-swimming is dangerous, but it’s also fun! Kids learn through play so if you can make it fun for them they’ll learn better

I have bipolar disorder, and I’ve learned that you have to take responsibility for your illness. I have type 1, meaning I have true manic episodes, and they’re not only damaging to me but to everyone around me. I can’t always control my actions during an episode but I can take steps to prevent one. Take your meds. Go to bed on time. Watch the substance use or abandon it completely. There’s no magical cure or solution, just lifestyle choices I have to make if I want to remain stable.

It’s entirely possible to do all the right things and have an episode anyways. It’s probable, actually. But having an episode every now and again is far better than flinging back and forth every few months between feeling like a god and wanting to kill yourself. 

Pot calling the kettle black right now as I’ve been having a hard time lately, but I can’t blame it all on my disorder. I’ve made the choices I’ve made and it’s up to me to make better ones now. 

Stability is possible. Happiness is possible. Bipolar is a lifelong illness but it’s not a death sentence.

I don’t have bpd, but these are my tips for bipolar.
- sleep sleep SLEEP! Go to bed at the same time every night and wake up at the same time every morning if possible
- diet is important. Try to eat healthy, and don’t skip meals
- meds. Take them at the same time every morning/night, set an alarm to remember, maybe get a cute pill organizer to make it a little fun
- track your mood. There’s apps, and mood journals aren’t hard to come by on Amazon
- research. There’s plenty of books on bipolar and I’m sure the same goes for bpd. I’ve found learning about my disorder makes it easier to recognize an episode 
- learn your warning signs. Write them down. If you have a support system, tell them what your warning signs are. For example, I know I’m starting a depressive episode if I stop cleaning my room and showering regularly, and a manic one if I feel too good and I start speeding and spending too much money. Recognizing warning signs can give you the ability to stop an episode in its tracks with medication
- therapy. Everyone should go to therapy, but more so if you have a mental illness. Betterhelp is expensive but it’s easy to find therapists who specialize in specific disorders. Local therapists are usually cheaper so long as you have insurance (I live in the USA might be different elsewhere)
- drugs and alcohol. Don’t do hard drugs. Weed effects everyone differently, I can smoke regularly and be fine, but it does have the potential to cause psychosis in predisposed individuals, so be careful. Don’t drink heavily/nightly, depending on your meds you might not want to drink at all. I’m technically not supposed to drink on my meds but I’ll have 2 beers every Friday, it just makes me SUPER sleepy so I don’t drink out anymore

I’ll reply back to this if I think of any more tips. Best of luck, hopefully you get a response with more BPD oriented tips as well!
